films.name: XP2

grainStructure.value: Chromogenic dye-cloud grain, softer and slightly coarser than XP2 Super's.

films.history: XP2 was Ilford's second chromogenic black-and-white film, sold from the 1990s until XP2 Super replaced it in the early 2000s. It was the first C-41 monochrome film many labs would process without argument, and its orange base made it a natural fit for scanning and minilab printing. Expired rolls usually still develop cleanly.

characteristics.label: Development
characteristics.value: C-41 only.

characteristics.label: Difference from Super
characteristics.value: Slightly coarser grain and a little less latitude.

films.name: Panatomic-X

grainStructure.value: Very fine conventional grain, among the finest of the mid-century emulsions.

films.history: Panatomic-X was Kodak's slow, ultra-fine black-and-white film from 1938 until it was discontinued in 1987. It was the landscape and architectural film of the mid-century, with a long straight line and almost no grain. Its replacement, Technical Pan, was sharper but far harder to use, and nothing since has quite the same gentle tonality.

characteristics.label: Grain
characteristics.value: Effectively grainless at 4×5 and very fine at 35 mm.

characteristics.label: Expired stock
characteristics.value: Usually fogged; rate slower and develop with a restrainer.

films.name: Portrait 160

grainStructure.value: Fine dye-cloud grain tuned for smooth skin rendering.

films.history: Agfa Portrait 160 was the professional portrait film of the Agfa-Gevaert range in the 1990s, designed for studio and wedding work with warm skin tones and a soft shoulder. It was discontinued with the rest of the professional line in 2005. Expired stock gives a gentle, slightly faded portrait palette.

characteristics.label: Skin
characteristics.value: Warm and smooth, with the softness the name promises.

films.name: RSX II 100

grainStructure.value: Fine dye-cloud grain on a neutral professional transparency.

films.history: Agfa RSX II 100 was the professional transparency of the Agfa range, sold through the 1990s until the company's collapse in 2005. It was warm and natural with clean skin tones, and it was the slide film many European studios used before Provia took over.

characteristics.label: Palette
characteristics.value: Warm and natural, less saturated than Velvia.

films.name: CTx 100
films.history: Agfa CTx 100 was the consumer transparency of the 1990s and 2000s, sold at a lower price than RSX II. It was warm and contrasty, and it was the slide film in a lot of European holiday cameras. It was discontinued in 2005.

characteristics.label: Cross-processing
characteristics.value: A cheap and common E-6-in-C-41 stock.

films.name: CHS 100 (original)

grainStructure.value: Single-layer conventional grain on a clear base, with no anti-halation layer.

films.history: The original Adox CHS 100 was a classic German emulsion from the 1950s, revived by Adox Photo Chemie in the 2000s and later replaced by CHS 100 II. It was thin-coated on a clear base with no anti-halation layer, so highlights bloom against dark backgrounds — the look people buy Adox for.

characteristics.label: Halation
characteristics.value: Strong, from the missing anti-halation layer.

characteristics.label: Developer
characteristics.value: Adonal or Rodinal at 1+50.

films.name: CHS 25

grainStructure.value: Very fine conventional grain on a clear base, with no anti-halation layer.

films.history: CHS 25 was the slowest of Adox's revived classic films, a very fine-grained emulsion intended for bright-light and copy work. It was discontinued in the 2010s. Developed in Rodinal 1+100 it gives extraordinary detail with a compensating tonality.

characteristics.label: Use
characteristics.value: Bright light, tripod, maximum resolution.

films.name: CMS 20

grainStructure.value: Microfilm emulsion, monodisperse and very thin.

films.history: CMS 20 was Adox's first version of its microfilm-based high-resolution film, sold before the II revision. It needed a special low-contrast developer to be usable, and its resolving power was unmatched. It was replaced by CMS 20 II.

characteristics.label: Developer
characteristics.value: Only a dedicated low-contrast developer gives a printable image.

films.name: Retro 100 Tonal

grainStructure.value: Fine conventional grain with a longer, softer curve than the other Retro films.

origin.note: Maco does not publish the coating source for the Retro films.

films.history: Retro 100 Tonal is a low-contrast version of Rollei's Retro 100, sold for work where a long and gentle tonal scale matters more than bite. It has the fine grain of the Retro family with a softer curve, and it is one of the more usable films in the range for portraits.

characteristics.label: Look
characteristics.value: Soft and tonal, with a long shoulder.

films.name: Crossbird 200

grainStructure.value: Fine dye-cloud grain on a colour transparency emulsion.

origin.note: Sold by Maco under the Rollei name; the coating source is not published. It is an E-6 transparency intended for cross-processing.

films.history: Rollei Crossbird 200 is a colour slide film sold by Maco and marketed for cross-processing. It is an E-6 film, so it can be shot as a slide, but its reason for existing is C-41: the saturated, shifted colours that E-6 stock gives in a negative process. Its coating source is not disclosed.

characteristics.label: Cross-processing
characteristics.value: Its intended use: E-6 film in C-41 for strong colour shifts.

characteristics.label: In E-6
characteristics.value: A conventional, slightly warm transparency.

films.name: Nightbird 400

grainStructure.value: Dye-cloud grain on a tungsten-balanced colour negative.

origin.note: A Maco/Rollei branded film; the coating is not published.

films.history: Nightbird 400 is a tungsten-balanced colour negative sold by Maco for night and available-light photography. It is balanced for 3200 K, so daylight needs an 85B filter, and its colour is tuned for artificial light. It is a niche film and is produced in small runs.

characteristics.label: Balance
characteristics.value: Tungsten 3200 K; an 85B filter is needed in daylight.

films.name: ATP 1.1

grainStructure.value: A technical panchromatic emulsion: extremely fine grain, very thin, with extended red sensitivity.

origin.note: Sold by Maco as a technical pan film; the coating source is not officially named.

films.history: Rollei ATP 1.1 is a technical panchromatic film: extremely fine-grained, very contrasty and extremely slow, sold for copy work, microscopy and any application where resolution matters more than tonality. It is widely believed to be based on Agfa's technical aerial stock and needs a low-contrast developer for pictorial use.

characteristics.label: Resolution
characteristics.value: Among the highest of any 35 mm film.

characteristics.label: Contrast
characteristics.value: Very high; a low-contrast developer or a compensating dilution is required.

films.name: NP 20

grainStructure.value: Not documented here. The name says only that it was slower than NP 27.

films.history: ORWO NP 20 was the slow black-and-white film of the Wolfen plant, one step below NP 22 and NP 27 in the range. The DX database gives its speed as 80 ASA, so the number in the name is an old East German rating rather than ISO 20. It went out of production after German reunification shrank the company.

characteristics.label: Speed
characteristics.value: 80 ASA in the DX database.

films.name: NP 27
films.history: ORWO NP 27 was the fast black-and-white film of the Wolfen plant's NP range, alongside NP 15, NP 20 and NP 22. The DX database rates it at 400 ASA and the published list of discontinued films gives ISO 400. The number in the name is an old East German rating rather than ISO 27. It is long discontinued.

characteristics.label: Speed
characteristics.value: 400 ASA in the DX database; ISO 400 in the published list.

films.name: Foto 65

grainStructure.value: Fine Soviet cubic grain with the thick coating and unevenness typical of Svema's production.

films.history: Svema Foto 65 was the fine-grain black-and-white film of the Soviet Union, made at Shostka and sold across the Eastern bloc. It was the slow, quality option next to Foto 100 and 200, and surviving stock is now decades expired. It is popular with people who want a genuinely unfamiliar look.

characteristics.label: Handling
characteristics.value: Thick and curly; load carefully and dry weighted.

characteristics.label: Expired stock
characteristics.value: Heavy fog; add a restrainer and develop cool.
